[Nehemiah] [12]:[35] Under [the leadership of] ZechariAh (son of JoNathan, grandson of ShemaiAh, son of MathaniJah, son of MichaiAh, son of ZacCur, son of Asaph), some of the of the Priests were blowing trumpets,
[Nehemiah] [12]:[36] while the rest of his family (ShemaiJah, AzaraEl, GilalAi, MaAi, NathaniEl, Judah, and HanaNi) walked behind Ezra the scribe playing the songs of David (the man of God) on their instruments.
[Nehemiah] [12]:[37] Then when they reached the Gate of the Spring, they marched down the stairway of the City of David and back up along the wall over the house of David, heading eastward towards the Water Gate.
[Nehemiah] [12]:[38] And as they were marching along [playing and singing their] songs of praise, the 2nd group was marching to meet them, as I walked behind them. Half of the people walked along the wall near the Furnace Tower, then along the Broad Wall
[Nehemiah] [12]:[39] over the Gate of Ephraim, and over the Gate of EiSiana, the Fish Gate, the Tower of HaNaneEl and the Tower of MeAh, all the way to the Sheep Gate, and then on to the Prison Gate,
[Nehemiah] [12]:[40] where both groups stopped to offer their praises at the Temple of God, as half of the commanders and I stood there.
[Nehemiah] [12]:[41] Then the Priests (EliAkim, MaAsiJah, MiniAmin, MichaiAh, ElioEnai, ZechariAh, and HanaNiJah) blew their trumpets,
[Nehemiah] [12]:[42] as MaAseJah, ShemiAh, EliEzer, UzZi, JehoHanan, MelchiJah, AiLam, Ezer (and their overseer, JezRahJah) started singing!
[Nehemiah] [12]:[43] Well, they offered many sacrifices that day and everyone was extremely happy, for God had made them, their wives, and their children very happy! And the sound of their joy could be heard a long distance from JeruSalem!
[Nehemiah] [12]:[44] It was on this day that they ordered those who were over the treasures in the treasuries (the first fruits and the tithes) to go out and gather the portions for the Priests and Levites from the cities and the fields. And everyone in Judah was very happy for the Priests, Levites, and the guards
[Nehemiah] [12]:[45] that kept the watches for their God, and for those in charge of the cleansing, for the singers, and for the gatekeepers, all of whom were doing everything according to the commandments of David and of his son Solomon.
[Nehemiah] [12]:[46] Because, it was in the days of David and Asaph that singers were first assigned to sing praises to God.
[Nehemiah] [12]:[47] And it was during the days of ZerubBabel and NehemiAh that all the people started contributing a portion to the singers and gatekeepers each day. It was handed over as something holy to the Levites, who handed it over as something holy to the sons of Aaron.
[Nehemiah] [13]:[1] Well on that day (when they were reading the scroll of Moses before the ears of the people), they came to understand that it was written that the AmMonites and MoAbites were not to enter the gathering of God throughout the ages,
[Nehemiah] [13]:[2] because they hadn’t greeted the sons of IsraEl with bread and water, but hired BalaAm to curse them (which our God turned into blessings).
[Nehemiah] [13]:[3] And when they heard this read in the Law, they separated such people who had been mixed among the IsraElites.
[Nehemiah] [13]:[4] Before that time, however, the Priest EliAshib had assigned TobiJah to be in charge of the treasury of the Temple of our God,
[Nehemiah] [13]:[5] [and he had moved into] the large room in the treasury where the sacrifice offerings, the frankincense, the sacred utensils, the tithe grain, the wine, and the olive oil was supposed to be stored (as it was commanded) for the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, along with the first fruits for the Priests.
[Nehemiah] [13]:[6] I wasn’t in JeruSalem when he did this, for (because it was the 32nd year of the reign of ArthaSastha the ruler of Babylon) I had gone to see the king, and then (after some time) I asked the king for a few things
[Nehemiah] [13]:[7] before returning to JeruSalem. But when I [got back and] saw the wicked thing that EliAshib had done for TobiJah by giving the treasury to him there in the courtyard of the Temple of God,
[Nehemiah] [13]:[8] this looked very wrong to me. So, I took all of TobiJah’s things out of the treasury and threw them outside!
[Nehemiah] [13]:[9] Then I gave the order and they cleansed the treasury, and I had the Temple of God’s sacred utensils, sacrifice offerings, and frankincense all brought back.
[Nehemiah] [13]:[10] I also realized that the Levites weren’t being given their portions, so the Levites, singers, and workmen had all returned to their own fields!
[Nehemiah] [13]:[11] Therefore, I had a heated exchange with those who were in charge, and I asked: ‘Why has the Temple of God been abandoned?’ And afterward, I called everyone back and assigned them to their stations,
[Nehemiah] [13]:[12] as everyone in Judah once again started bringing their tithes of the wheat, wine, and olive oil to the treasury.
[Nehemiah] [13]:[13] I then put all of this into the hands of the Priest ShelemiJah, the scribe ZaDok, and PedaiAh and Hanan (the sons of ZacCur and grandsons of MatTaniJah) who represented the Levites, since I thought that they could be trusted. And I left it up to them to divide it all among their brothers.
[Nehemiah] [13]:[14] Remember me for this, O my God, and don’t forget my acts of mercy on behalf of the Temple of my God [Jehovah] and [the assignment of] His watches!
[Nehemiah] [13]:[15] Well, it was then that I noticed that the people of Judah were treading their wine vats and collecting sheaves of grain and loading them on their burros (along with wine, grapes, figs, and everything else) and carrying them into JeruSalem on the Sabbath day! Yes, I can testify to the fact that they were even selling these things on that day!
[Nehemiah] [13]:[16] People from Tyre were also bringing in fish and all sorts of things, and they were sitting there offering them for sale to the sons of Judah in JeruSalem on the Sabbath!
[Nehemiah] [13]:[17] So I quarreled with the free men of Judah and asked: ‘Why are you doing this wicked thing… Why are you profaning the day of the Sabbath?
[Nehemiah] [13]:[18] ‘Isn’t this the same thing that your fathers did that caused God to bring all the evils down upon this city and upon us? ‘Now you’re adding to His anger upon IsraEl by profaning the Sabbath!’
[Nehemiah] [13]:[19] Well, after I said that, they started locking the gates of JeruSalem before the Sabbath, and I told them not to unlock them until after the Sabbath. Then I had some of my young men stand at the gates to make sure that no one carried loads on the Sabbath day,
[Nehemiah] [13]:[20] and that all the traders were forced to find lodging. Oh, some did business outside of JeruSalem’s walls once or twice,
[Nehemiah] [13]:[21] but I spoke to them and asked: ‘Why are you lodging so close to the city wall? ‘If you do this a second time, I’ll be forced to take action against you!’ Well from that time on, they no longer came on the Sabbath.
[Nehemiah] [13]:[22] Thereafter, I had a talk with the Levites who were being cleansed and with those who had come to guard the gates, about the need to keep the Sabbath day holy. Remember me, O my God, and protect me by Your great mercy!
[Nehemiah] [13]:[23] Back then, I saw Judeans that had settled in with women who were AshDodites, AmMonites, and MoAbites…
[Nehemiah] [13]:[24] They were even speaking the AshDod language and they weren’t learning Judean, for they were speaking the languages of these people and those people!
[Nehemiah] [13]:[25] So I quarreled with them and I cursed them… I hit some of the men, pulled their hair, and made them swear before God not to take those people’s daughters for their sons or for themselves.
[Nehemiah] [13]:[26] [I said]: ‘Isn’t this how Solomon the king of IsraEl sinned? ‘Yet among all the nations, there wasn’t another king like him, because God loved him and God appointed him to be the king over all IsraEl. ‘But it was this thing that turned him aside… Foreign women!
[Nehemiah] [13]:[27] ‘So, should we allow you to do such wickedness and break your relationship with God by taking foreign women?’
[Nehemiah] [13]:[28] [I said this to] the sons of JoiAda and to EliAshib (who was the High Priest and a relative by marriage of SanBalLat)… Then I threw them all out!
[Nehemiah] [13]:[29] Remember them, O my God, because they opposed the rights of inheritance of the Priesthood [as was set forth in] Your Sacred Agreement for the Priests and the Levites!
[Nehemiah] [13]:[30] I cleansed them of all their connections with foreigners, then I established the daily rotations for the Priests and Levites, so that every man had an assignment among the Priests,
[Nehemiah] [13]:[31] whether it was just to provide gifts of wood for the offerings by seasons and times, or [to bring in] the first fruits. Please remember me, O our God, for the goodness that [I have shown]!
[Esther] [1]:[1] In the second year of King ArtaXerxes’ reign, the great ruler, on the 1st day of Nisan, MordecAi had [a] dream. He was JaiRus’s son, Shimei’s grandson, and Kish’s great-grandson, from Benjamin’s tribe. 1.2 He was [a] Jewish man, living in the city of Susa. He was [a] prominent man who served in the king’s court. 1.3 He had been among those captured by NebuChadnezzar, Babylon’s king, from JeruSalem, along with JeconiAh, Judea’s king. 1.4 Here’s what he dreamed: Suddenly, there were voices, a commotion, thunder, an earthquake, and widespread chaos across the earth. 1.5 Then, he saw two great dragons appear, ready to fight each other... They let out [a] great roar, 1.6 and because of their roar, every nation prepared for war, ready to fight against [a] nation of the righteous. 1.7 Then came [a] day of darkness and gloom, trouble and distress, great suffering, and widespread chaos across the earth. 1.8 Every righteous nation became troubled. They feared their impending doom and expected to die. 1.9 So they cried out to The God! From their cries, [a] great river emerged, as if from [a] small spring, with abundant water. 1.10 Then light appeared and the sun rose, and the humble were exalted and overcame the glorious ones. 1.11 When MordecAi woke up, he had seen this dream and understood what The God intended to do. He kept it in mind and pondered it until nightfall, trying to understand it completely. 1.12 [Later,] MordecAi was then resting in the [King’s] court with the two king’s eunuchs who guarded the court, Gabatha and Tharra. 1.13 Well, he overheard their conversation and got an insight into their concerns... He learned they were preparing to attack King ArtaXerxes! So he reported them to the king. 1.14 The king questioned the two eunuchs, and when they confessed, they were executed. 1.15 The king had these events recorded, and MordecAi also wrote about these matters. 1.16 The king then ordered MordecAi to serve in the court and rewarded him with gifts for these actions. 1.17 Now, HaMan (son of HamaDathus the Bugaean) was greatly honored by the king. He tried to harm MordecAi and his people because of the two king’s eunuchs. 1.18 So [the following] happened after these events, during King ArtaXerxes’ reign (this ArtaXerxes ruled over 127 provinces, extending from India):
[Esther] [1]:[2] In these days, when ArtaXerxes was ruling as king in the City of Susa,
[Esther] [1]:[3] during the 3rd year of his reign, he held a great [wedding] banquet to which he invited his friends, foreign dignitaries, the most honorable Medes and Persians, and those who were in charge of the governors of the various regions.
[Esther] [1]:[4] Then, over the next 180 days, he took them and showed them all the wealth of his kingdom and the glory of the things that he’d accomplished.
[Esther] [1]:[5] Well, after the days for celebrating his wedding were completed, the king held another banquet inside the courtyard of the king’s palace for the foreigners who lived in his city, which lasted 7 more days.
[Esther] [1]:[6] The [banquet] area was decorated with fine linen and cotton cloth that was stretched over lines of fine linen and purple cloth, which were fastened with gold and silver cubes to Parian-marble columns.
[Esther] [1]:[7] [There were also] beds of gold and silver on a Parian-marble floor [that was set with] emerald stones and mother of pearl, and this was strewn with transparent beds that were variously decorated with cups of gold and silver. In addition, they had an abundance of the finest wines (the type that was reserved for the king).
[Esther] [1]:[8] The banquet wasn’t handled as it was specified in their laws, but because that’s the way the king wanted it, he gave instructions to those who were in charge of the workers to handle things his way.
[Esther] [1]:[9] Meanwhile, Astin (the queen) was holding a banquet for the women of the kingdom in the same place where ArtaXerxes was holding his.
[Esther] [1]:[10] Then on the 7th day, because the king was in a particularly happy mood, he gave orders to HaMan, BizTha, Harbona, BigTha, AbagTha, Zethar, and Carcas (the king’s 7 [most trusted] eunuchs) to bring the queen to him,
[Esther] [1]:[11] so she could receive her coronation and be given a royal turban, and so that he could display her beauty before all the princes and the foreigners (because she was very beautiful).
[Esther] [1]:[12] But Queen Astin refused to go along with the eunuchs, which made the king very angry.
[Esther] [1]:[13] So he said to his friends: ‘If this is how Astin has chosen to answer, then you deal with this matter according to the law and judge her!’
[Esther] [1]:[14] Well, Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, TarShish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan (the 7 sub-rulers of the Persians and Medes who were closest to the king and who sat by him) came forward
[Esther] [1]:[15] and told the king what the laws required them to do to Queen Astin for not following the orders that the king had given to his eunuchs.
[Esther] [1]:[16] Memucan spoke and said this to him and to the other rulers: ‘Not only has Queen Astin dishonored the king, but she has dishonored all of the king’s rulers and leaders.’
[Esther] [1]:[17] Then after describing to them all the things that the queen had said and how she had disobeyed the king, he proclaimed: ‘Because she has disobeyed King ArtaXerxes,
[Esther] [1]:[18] and because all the wives of the sub-rulers and leaders of the Persians and Medes have heard what the queen said, they might also dare to dishonor their husbands!
[Esther] [1]:[19] ‘Therefore, if it seems good to the king, let him write out and sign a royal decree passing a law among the Medes and Persians that she should not be treated as the queen and that she may no longer sleep with the king. ‘Then may the king find a woman better than her!
[Esther] [1]:[20] ‘This law should be announced throughout the entire kingdom, so that all the women will learn to respect their men, both the rich and the poor!’
[Esther] [1]:[21] Well, because what he said pleased the king and his rulers, the king did as Memucan had proposed...
[Esther] [1]:[22] He sent a proclamation everywhere throughout his entire realm in each of their languages, requiring women to show respect for the men in their households.
[Esther] [2]:[1] This ended the king’s rage, and he never mentioned Astin again, or the things that she said, or his condemnation of her.
[Esther] [2]:[2] So then the king’s servants said to him: ‘Have them search for a young woman for the king who is both pure and beautiful to look at.
[Esther] [2]:[3] ‘Send judges throughout your kingdom and have them choose young women who are virgins and pretty, then have them taken to your harem in the City of Susa where they’ll be handed over to the king’s eunuch that’s in charge of the women, to take care of them and give them beauty treatments.
[Esther] [2]:[4] ‘And after that, the woman who best pleases the king will reign instead of Astin.’ Well, because this pleased the king, it was done.
[Esther] [2]:[5] Now, there was a man (a Judean) in the City of Susa whose name was MordecAi. He was the son of JaiRus, the grandson of SemeYas, and the great-grandson of KisaYus from the tribe of BenJamin,
[Esther] [2]:[6] who had been carried off as a captive from JeruSalem by NebuChadnezzar, the king of Babylon.
[Esther] [2]:[7] MordecAi had a child whom he’d raised who was the daughter of his uncle (his father’s brother), and her name was Esther. For after her parents died, he [agreed to] take [care of] the young woman, who was very pretty.
[Esther] [2]:[8] Well, after the king’s proclamation [was read], many young women were gathered to the City of Susa [to be seen by] Gai (the harem keeper), and then Esther was led before him...
[Esther] [2]:[9] He found the young woman very pleasing and he liked her, so he hurried to give her the beauty treatments and her share [of good things], and 7 young women from the royal palace were brought there [to serve] her. Thereafter, he treated [Esther] and her handmaidens very well in the harem chamber.
[Esther] [2]:[10] However, Esther didn’t discuss her race or her fatherland with him, because MordecAi had told her not to mention it.
[Esther] [2]:[11] Then, every day, MordecAi would walk by the women’s courtyard to see what was happening to Esther.
[Esther] [2]:[12] Well, at the end of 12 months, the time finally came for the young women to go in to the king (for that’s how long the beauty treatments were to last). They also underwent 6 months of treatments with fragrant oils.
[Esther] [2]:[13] It was then, after 6 months of being bathed in myrrh oil, that she was taken in to the king, along with any others that the king told them to bring from the harem chamber to the royal palace.
[Esther] [2]:[14] She was brought in to him that evening, and the next morning, she returned to the secondary harem where the Eunuch Gai (the king’s harem keeper) stayed, and she couldn’t go before the king after that, unless she had been called.
[Esther] [2]:[15] Well eventually, Esther (the daughter of AbiHail, MordecAi’s uncle) was brought before the king again, and she carefully followed all the eunuch’s instructions, so that everyone who saw her came to like her.
[Esther] [2]:[16] Esther had been taken to King ArtaXerxes in the 10th month (TeBeth) of the 7th year of his reign,
[Esther] [2]:[17] and he fell passionately in love with her, preferring her to all the other virgins! He then placed the royal turban of the queen on her head,
[Esther] [2]:[18] and he held a banquet for all of his friends and the governors that lasted 7 days. He also made the wedding feast of Esther greater by [releasing all the prisoners] in his kingdom.
[Esther] [2]:[19] Meanwhile, MordecAi had been put in charge of matters having to do with [the king’s] courtyard.
[Esther] [2]:[20] And he reminded Esther not to mention her fatherland. Rather, he told her to just fear God and obey His orders, the same as she did when she lived in his home… And Esther never deviated from doing this.
[Esther] [2]:[21] Well, MordecAi kept growing more important,
[Esther] [2]:[22] and when two of the king’s eunuchs (the chiefs of his bodyguards) became worried about ArtaXerxes and decided to assassinate him, MordecAi heard about this and sent a warning to the king through Esther about their plot.
[Esther] [2]:[23] So after the king interrogated the eunuchs, he had them hung, and he had a record written in the royal library about the goodwill that MordecAi had shown, saying that he was to be commended for this.
[Esther] [3]:[1] However, after that, King ArtaXerxes honored HaMan (son of AmaDathes the AgAgite). He promoted him over all his friends and seated him in [the most prominent position].
[Esther] [3]:[2] So thereafter, everyone in the courtyard had to bow before HaMan, because the king said that they had to do so… However, MordecAi refused to do this.
[Esther] [3]:[3] As a result, the people in the king’s courtyard started asking MordecAi why he was disobeying the order of the king.
[Esther] [3]:[4] And although they spoke to him about this every day, MordecAi just didn’t pay any attention to them... So someone thereafter pointed out to HaMan that MordecAi had been disobeying the king’s orders, and he also mentioned that MordecAi was a Judean.
[Esther] [3]:[5] Well, when HaMan found out that MordecAi wasn’t bowing before him, this made him very angry!
[Esther] [3]:[6] So, that’s when he started making plans to remove all the Judeans from the kingdom of ArtaXerxes.
[Esther] [3]:[7] Then, during the 12th year of the reign of ArtaXerxes, he drafted a law, and he threw lots for each day and month to determine when the best time would be to destroy the race of MordecAi… And it fell on the 14th day of the month of Adar.
[Esther] [3]:[8] So he went and spoke to King ArtaXerxes and said this: ‘There’s a nation that’s mixed among all the nations of your kingdom whose laws are different from those of the other nations, and they disregard the laws of the king! ‘Therefore, it isn’t to the king’s advantage to keep them...
[Esther] [3]:[9] So if it seems good to the king; may he approve this decree [that I’ve written], which says that they must be destroyed! ‘Then I’ll appropriate 10,000 gold coins from the king’s treasury to get it done.’
[Esther] [3]:[10] Well, the king removed his ring and handed it to HaMan to seal the judgment that he had written against the Judeans.
[Esther] [3]:[11] And the king said to HaMan: ‘As for the [money]; you have it. ‘And as for that nation; treat them in any way that you wish!’
[Esther] [3]:[12] So then the king called in his scribes (on the 13th day of the 1st month) and they copied HaMan’s orders [and sent them to] all the military commanders and governors from India to Ethiopia… To 127 districts. [HaMan also] sent letters to all the rulers of the nations in their own languages in the name of King ArtaXerxes.
[Esther] [3]:[13] He sent them by couriers throughout ArtaXerxes’s kingdom, [telling the people] to wipe out the race of the Judeans on a single day in the 12th month (Adar), and he told them that they could plunder all their possessions. Here is a copy of the letter: 13.1 ‘Great King ArtaXerxes sends this message to the satraps and governors of the 127 provinces, from India to Ethiopia, who are under his rule: 13.2 ‘I have ruled over many nations and taken control of the entire inhabited world. I have not wished to be arrogant in my power, but always to govern fairly and gently. My aim has been to ensure lasting peace for those under my rule, to make the kingdom gentle and easily accessible everywhere, and to restore the peace longed for by all humanity. 13.3 ‘When I asked my advisors how to achieve this, HaMan — who has proven himself wise among us, has shown unwavering loyalty and strong faithfulness, and who holds the second highest rank in the kingdom — 13.4 informed us that a certain hostile group of people is scattered among all the other groups throughout the inhabited world. ‘Their laws differ from those of every other nation, and they constantly ignore the king’s orders. This prevents our government from operating smoothly and flawlessly. 13.5 ‘So, we understand that this nation is completely unique, always in opposition to everyone else, with strange and distinct laws. They are hostile to our interests, causing great harm and preventing the kingdom from becoming stable. 13.6 ‘Therefore, we have ordered that the people HaMan identified in his writings to you — HaMan, who manages our affairs and is our chief minister — be completely destroyed. This includes men, women, and children, by their enemies’ swords, without any mercy or sympathy, on the 14th day of the 12th month, Adar, of the current year. 13.7 ‘This is so that these people (who have been hostile both in the past and now) will be violently sent to the Place of the Dead on a single day. ‘This will ensure a stable and peaceful government for us forever.’
[Esther] [3]:[14] So, copies of the letters were put on display everywhere... And then the day was set and everything was being prepared and made ready…
[Esther] [3]:[15] Even in Susa. And after that, the king and HaMan toasted each other, as the whole city was in an uproar.
[Esther] [4]:[1] Well when MordecAi realized that this was the end, he ripped his clothes, put on sackcloth, [covered himself with] ashes, and he rushed to the city square, where he yelled as loudly as he could: ‘A nation is being removed that has wronged no one!’
[Esther] [4]:[2] Then after that, he went and stood outside the palace gate (because he wasn’t allowed to enter the courtyard in sackcloth and ashes).
[Esther] [4]:[3] And everywhere that the letters were on display there was crying, beating on chests, and great mourning among the Judeans, as they put on sackcloth and made beds for themselves in ashes.
[Esther] [4]:[4] Well, the queen soon learned about this plot through her handmaids and eunuchs, who came to her and told her about it… And she was very upset when she heard what had happened. Meanwhile, she sent a robe to MordecAi and told him to stop wearing his sackcloth; but he refused to do it.
[Esther] [4]:[5] Then Esther called Hatach (her personal eunuch) and sent him to MordecAi,
[Esther] [4]:[6] so she could learn the details of the situation.
[Esther] [4]:[7] And MordecAi explained to him how it all came about… Of how HaMan had gotten the king’s promise to receive 10,000 gold coins from his treasury so he could destroy the Judeans...
[Esther] [4]:[8] And then he gave a copy of the decree that was on public display in Susa (which said that they were to be destroyed) to Hatach, who carried it to Esther. He also told the eunuch to ask her to [go before] the king [to beg for his mercy] and for her to prove worthy by speaking on behalf of her people. He said: ‘Tell her to explain to him about how lowly she was once considered and of how I took her in and raised her, because HaMan (the king’s second in command) is talking about killing all of us. ‘Tell her to call upon the Lord [our God], and then go speak to the king about us and rescue us from death!’
[Esther] [4]:[9] So Hatach returned and told Esther everything that [Modecai] had said.
[Esther] [4]:[10] And then Esther told Hatach to go to MordecAi and say: ‘Everyone in the kingdom knows that there’s no hope for any man or woman who goes into the king’s inner courtyard without being called [first].
[Esther] [4]:[11] Only those to whom the king stretches out his scepter is safe… And I haven’t been called to see the king for some 30 days now!’
[Esther] [4]:[12] Therefore, Hatach went and told MordecAi everything that Esther said, and MordecAi told him:
[Esther] [4]:[13] ‘Go and tell Esther not to think that she’s the only Judean who’ll be saved.
[Esther] [4]:[14] And if she wants to ignore us this time, the Judeans will get help from somewhere else… Then she and the house of her father will be destroyed! ‘But... Perhaps she was made queen for this very purpose?’
[Esther] [4]:[15] Then Esther sent a reply to MordecAi, saying:
[Esther] [4]:[16] ‘Gather all the Judeans in the City of Susa and ask everyone to fast for me… Don’t eat or drink anything for three days and three nights! ‘Also, my handmaids and I will go without food before I go in before the king, because I’ll be breaking the law. ‘Yet, even if it’s necessary for me to die, I’ll do it!’
[Esther] [4]:[17] And thereafter, MordecAi did everything that Esther told him to do. 17.1 Then he prayed to [Jehovah], remembering all of [Jehovah’s] actions, and said: 17.2 ‘O [Jehovah], O [Jehovah], ‘King who rules over everything, because everything is in His power, and no one can stop Him when He plans to save Israel! 17.3‘After all, He made the heavens and the earth and all the wonders under the sky, 17.4 and He is [Jehovah] over everything; no one can resist Him, the Lord! 17.5 ‘You know everything, O [Jehovah]. ‘You know that I did this — refusing to bow down before the arrogant HaMan — not because of disrespect, pride, or [a] desire for glory. 17.6 Indeed, I would have willingly humbled myself before him to save Israel, 17.7 but I did this because I didn’t want to put human glory above God’s glory. ‘I won’t bow down to anyone but You, my Lord, and I’m not acting proudly in this situation. 17.8 ‘Now, O [Jehovah], The God, the King, The God of Abraham... ‘Spare Your people, because they’re determined to destroy us and have wanted to wipe out Your inheritance from the start! 17.9‘Don’t abandon Your own people, whom You rescued for Yourself from Egypt... 17.10 Hear my plea and be kind to Your chosen people. Turn our mourning into feasting, so that as long as we live, we can sing praises to Your name, O [Jehovah], and don’t silence those who praise You.’ 17.11 All Israel cried out with all their strength, because death was staring them in the face. 17.12 Queen Esther also found refuge in the Lord, overwhelmed by the fear of death. 17.13 She took off her splendid robes and put on clothes indicating distress and mourning. Instead of her expensive perfumes, she covered her head with ashes and dung. She deeply humbled herself, and instead of beautiful jewelry, she now had tangled hair. 17.14 She pleaded with [Jehovah], Israel’s God, saying: 17.15 ‘My Lord, our King, You alone exist. ‘Help me, because I’m alone and have no one to help me but You, 17.16 because I’m risking my life. 17.17‘Since I was born, within my family’s tribe, I’ve heard that You, O [Jehovah], chose Israel from all the nations and our fathers from all their ancestors to be Your eternal inheritance, and You did everything You promised for them. 17.18 ‘Now we’ve sinned before You, and You’ve handed us over to our enemies; 17.19 because we honored their gods. You are righteous, O [Jehovah]. 17.20‘But now, they’re not satisfied with how harshly we’re enslaved; instead, they’ve acted against us, to cancel Your command and destroy Your inheritance, to silence those who praise You and to extinguish the glory of Your house and Your altar, 17.21 and to make nations praise worthless idols and worship [a] mortal king into the age! 17.22 ‘Don’t hand over Your scepter, O [Jehovah], to those who are worthless, and don’t let them mock our ruin. ‘Instead, turn their plans back on them! And make an example of the one who started this against us! 17.23‘Remember us, O [Jehovah], show Your power in our time of trouble, and give me courage, O King of the gods and ruler over all power. 17.24‘Put the right words in my mouth when I face the ‘lion’, and make him hate the one who fights against us, so he’ll be destroyed, along with everyone who agrees with him. 17.25‘But deliver us by Your hand, and help me, because I’m alone and have no one but You, O [Jehovah]. You know everything, 17.26 and You know I hate the glory of lawless people, and I despise sleeping with uncircumcised men or any foreigner. 17.27‘You know my suffering, that I hate the symbol of my high position, which I wear on my head during public appearances. I hate it like [a] menstrual rag, and I don’t wear it on my personal days! 17.28‘Your servant hasn’t eaten at HaMan’s table, nor have I attended the king’s banquet, nor have I drunk wine offered to idols; 17.29 And your servant hasn’t found any joy since the day I was changed, except in You, O [Jehovah], The God of Abraham. 17.30 ‘O The God, who is mighty over everything, hear the cries of those in despair and rescue us from those who act wickedly, and rescue me from my fear.’
[Esther] [5]:[1] On the third day, after finishing her prayers, she changed out of her prayer clothes and into her royal robes... 1.2 After getting ready and praying to The God (who protects and saves everyone), she brought her two attendants with her, 1.3 gently leaning on one of them, 1.4 while the other followed, helping to hold up her long dress. 1.5 Even though she was at the height of her beauty, with a blush, and her face appeared cheerful and pleasant, her mind was gripped by fear. 1.6 After passing through all the doors, she stood before the king... He sat on his royal throne, wearing his magnificent robes, completely adorned with gold and precious stones, and he appeared extremely intimidating! 1.7 He lifted his face, which shone brightly and was full of intense anger, and looked at her. The queen collapsed, turning pale and faint, and rested her head on the handmaiden supporting her. 1.8But The God softened the king’s attitude. Distressed, he quickly rose from his throne and took her into his arms until she recovered, comforting her with soothing words. He said to her: 1.9 ‘What’s wrong, Esther? I’m your brother; be brave! 1.10 ‘You won’t die, because this decree is ordinary. 1.11 ‘Come closer.’
[Esther] [5]:[2] He then raised his golden scepter and touched it against her neck. He kissed her and said: ‘Speak to me.’ 2.13 She replied: ‘My lord, ‘I saw you like [a] messenger of God, and my mind was troubled because your splendor terrified me! 2.14‘You are truly awe-inspiring, my lord, and your face shows great loving kindness.’ 2.15 But as she spoke, she fainted! 2.16 The king was distressed, and all his attendants comforted her.
[Esther] [5]:[3] Then the king asked: ‘What do you want Esther… What’s your request? ‘Ask for half of my kingdom and it’s yours.’
[Esther] [5]:[4] And Esther said: ‘This is a special day for me... So if it seems good to the king, may both the king and HaMan attend a banquet that I will hold for them today!’
[Esther] [5]:[5] So the king said to HaMan: ‘Hurry, let’s go and do what Esther has asked!’ And they both went to the banquet that Esther had prepared.
[Esther] [5]:[6] Well, when they arrived, the king said to Esther: ‘Tell me what it is that’s so important to you, Queen Esther, and I’ll do whatever is worthwhile.’
[Esther] [5]:[7] Then she said: ‘My only request and petition is this:
[Esther] [5]:[8] ‘If I’ve found the favor of the king, may you and HaMan come again tomorrow for [another] banquet that I’ll hold for you, the same as today.’
[Esther] [5]:[9] Well after HaMan left the king that day, he was very cheerful and happy. But when he noticed the Judean MordecAi standing in the courtyard, he was furious.
[Esther] [5]:[10] Then when he got home, he called his wife ZoSara and his friends,
[Esther] [5]:[11] and he showed them all the wealth he’d gained. He also told them of the glory that the king had vested upon him, and of how the king had appointed him to be the most important and how he had given him the lead position in his kingdom.
[Esther] [5]:[12] Then HaMan said: ‘Today, the queen didn’t invite anyone to a banquet that she held other than just me and the king, and she has invited me again tomorrow!
[Esther] [5]:[13] ‘However, the thing that really bothered me was seeing that Jew – MordecAi – standing there in the courtyard!’
[Esther] [5]:[14] Then his wife ZoSara said to him and his friends: ‘You should cut down a very tall tree, then at dawn tomorrow morning, you should go and speak to the king about hanging MordecAi on it, so that when you attend the banquet with the king, you can do it joyfully!’ Well, because this seemed to be a good idea, HaMan went and prepared the tree.
[Esther] [6]:[1] However, because the Lord [God] had removed sleep from the king that night, he gave orders to his servant to bring in the memorandum letters and to read them to him.
[Esther] [6]:[2] And that’s when he found the letter concerning MordecAi, which told of how he’d reported that two of the king’s eunuchs were looking to get their hands on ArtaXerxes.
[Esther] [6]:[3] So the king asked: ‘What glory or favor was shown to MordecAi for doing this?’ And the king’s servants replied: ‘Nothing has been done for him.’
[Esther] [6]:[4] Well, it so happened that, just as the king was asking about doing good things for MordecAi, {Look!} HaMan arrived in the courtyard... For he’d come to speak to the king about hanging MordecAi on the pole that he had prepared! So the king asked: ‘Who is in the courtyard?’
[Esther] [6]:[5] And the king’s servants replied: ‘Look, its HaMan standing in the courtyard.’ And the king said: ‘Call him in!’
[Esther] [6]:[6] Then the king asked HaMan: ‘Tell me... What [would you suggest that] I do for a man whom I wish to honor?’ Well, HaMan thought to himself: ‘Whom would the king wish to honor other than me?’
[Esther] [6]:[7] So he said to the king: ‘As for the man whom the king wishes to honor...
[Esther] [6]:[8] ‘The king’s servants should bring him the same fine linen that the king wears, as well as the king’s horse.
[Esther] [6]:[9] ‘Then one of the king’s most honored friends should dress the man who is loved by the king in royal robes, mount him on the horse, and then lead him around the city square proclaiming: ‘This is how any man who is honored by the king must be treated!’
[Esther] [6]:[10] And at that, the king said to HaMan: ‘Well spoken! ‘That’s what I want you to do for my courtyard attendant, the Jew MordecAi… ‘Be sure that you do everything that you said!’
[Esther] [6]:[11] Well thereafter, HaMan went and got the robes and the horse, then he dressed MordecAi and mounted him on the [king’s] horse, and he led him around the city square proclaiming: ‘This is how any man who is honored by the king must be treated!’
[Esther] [6]:[12] And after he brought MordecAi back to the courtyard, he went home extremely upset and with a worried mind.
[Esther] [6]:[13] So when he got back home, he told his wife ZoSara and his friends everything that had happened. Then his wife and friends said: ‘Since MordecAi is of the Judean race and you’ve started being humbled before him, this means that you’re going to fall… ‘There’s no way to defend yourself against that man, because the Living God is with him!’
[Esther] [6]:[14] Well, it was while they were still speaking to him that the eunuchs arrived to hurry HaMan along to the banquet that had been prepared by Esther.
[Esther] [7]:[1] So then, the king and HaMan went in to [eat and] drink with the queen on the 2nd day of the banquet,
[Esther] [7]:[2] and the king asked Esther: ‘What would you like, Queen Esther? ‘What’s your request or petition? ‘Whatever you may ask is yours… Up to half of my kingdom!’
[Esther] [7]:[3] And she replied: ‘If I’ve found favor before the king, my request and petition is for him to grant life to my people...
[Esther] [7]:[4] ‘For my people and I have been sold for destruction, ravaging, and as male and female slaves… Including our children! ‘I haven’t mentioned this to you before, but the one who slandered us is no longer worthy to sit in the courtyard of the king.’
[Esther] [7]:[5] Well at that, the king asked: ‘Who would have dared to do such a thing?’
[Esther] [7]:[6] And Esther said: ‘A man… An enemy… HaMan… This wicked man!’ Well, HaMan became very upset before the king and queen,
[Esther] [7]:[7] and the king just got up and walked out into the garden. So then HaMan appealed to the queen, because he saw that he was in a bad situation.
[Esther] [7]:[8] Then when the king returned from the garden, he found that HaMan had fallen on the queen’s bed as he was begging her. And the king asked: ‘Are you attacking my wife here in my own home?’ Well when HaMan heard that, he didn’t know what to say.
[Esther] [7]:[9] Then Harbonah (one of the king’s eunuchs) said to the king: '{Look!} HaMan has prepared a very tall pole [on which he’s planned to hang] MordecAi, the man who protected the king… ‘He had it erected next to his home.’ And the king said: ‘Then let him be hung on it!’
[Esther] [7]:[10] So HaMan was hung on the pole that he’d prepared for MordecAi that day, and this ended the king’s rage.
[Esther] [8]:[1] Then on that same day, King ArtaXerxes offered everything that had once belonged to the slanderer HaMan, to Esther. And after Esther explained how MordecAi was related to her, the king called him in
[Esther] [8]:[2] and gave him the ring that he’d removed from the hand of HaMan! Esther also put MordecAi in charge of all the possessions of HaMan.
[Esther] [8]:[3] Then, later that day, [Esther] went in and spoke to the king. She fell to his feet and begged him to undo all the evil things that HaMan had [planned] to do against the Judeans.
[Esther] [8]:[4] So the king held out his gold scepter to Esther, and she got up on her feet and stood next to the king and said:
[Esther] [8]:[5] ‘If it seems good to you, and if I’ve found your favor; have those letters that HaMan wrote and sent out about destroying all the Judeans in your kingdom, recalled.
[Esther] [8]:[6] ‘For, how could I watch my people being so mistreated, and how could I personally be saved when everyone else in my fatherland is being destroyed?’
[Esther] [8]:[7] But the king said to Esther: ‘Since I’ve already granted you everything that HaMan owned, and I had him hung on a pole for raising his hands against the Judeans, what more are you asking?
[Esther] [8]:[8] ‘You may write whatever seems good to you in my name and then seal it with my ring. However, once the king has given an order and has sealed it with his ring, it may never be changed!’
[Esther] [8]:[9] Well, it was the 23rd day of the 1st month (Nisan) of the same year that the scribes were called in, and [an edict] was written concerning the Judeans that was thereafter sent to all those in authority... To those who were in charge and to all the governors from India to Ethiopia, 127 governors by districts, in each of their own languages.
[Esther] [8]:[10] It was written in the name of the king, sealed with his ring, and sent out by couriers.
[Esther] [8]:[11] It gave instructions on how his laws were to be executed in each city, and explained that [the Judeans] should be helped in dealing with their opponents and enemies in any way they wanted,
[Esther] [8]:[12] all on a single day, throughout the entire kingdom of ArtaXerxes, on the 13th day of the 12th month (Adar)... 12.1 The following is [a] copy of the letter: ‘King ArtaXerxes the Great, to the rulers of the 127 satrapies from India to Ethiopia, and to those who support us, greetings. 12.2 ‘Many people, after often receiving great kindness from those who helped them, have become arrogant. 12.3 And, unable to control their own insolence, they not only try to harm our subjects, but also plot against the very people who helped them. 12.4 They don’t just eliminate gratitude among people. Instead, inflated by the boasts of the ungrateful, they imagine they can escape the judgment of God, who is always watching and hates evil. 12.5 Often, also, such malice has led many officials, who were trusted to manage the affairs of friends, to become involved in innocent bloodshed through false accusations, entangling them in terrible troubles. 12.6 This happens because of malicious and false reasoning, as they deceived those in power, who had pure intentions. 12.7 ‘You can see this, not only from the older histories we’ve passed down, but more clearly from the many wicked acts you yourselves have witnessed firsthand, resulting from the destructive influence of unworthy rulers. 12.8 We are determined to monitor future events, so we can provide a peaceful and stable kingdom for everyone, 12.9 by adapting to changes and always addressing new developments more fairly. 12.10 ‘Indeed, HaMan, son of HamaDatha, [a] Macedonian, was truly foreign to Persian blood and far from our goodness. Yet, we welcomed him as a guest, 12.11 and he received the same kindness we extend to every nation. In fact, he was even called our father and everyone continued to bow down to him as the second in command of the kingdom. 12.12 But he could not tolerate his own arrogance. So, he plotted to seize our rule and even our very breath, 12.13 and, using intricate and deceptive methods, he tried to destroy MordecAi, our savior and constant helper, and Esther, our blameless royal partner, along with their entire nation. 12.14 He believed that by doing this, he could render us helpless and then transfer control of the Persian Empire to the Macedonians. 12.15 ‘However, we’ve found that the Jews, whom this exceedingly wicked man had marked for annihilation, are not evildoers. Instead, they live by very righteous laws, 12.16 and are indeed Most High’s children, the greatest, living The God, Who has guided our kingdom and our ancestors’ kingdom with the utmost care. 12.17 ‘Therefore, you should not use the letters HaMan, son of HamaDatha, sent, 12.18 because the man who planned all this was executed at the gates of Susa with his entire household. The all-prevailing The God swiftly delivered the judgment he deserved. 12.19 ‘You are to boldly publish [a] copy of this letter everywhere, permitting the Jews to live by their own laws, 12.20 and support them so they can defend themselves against their attackers during their time of trouble, on the 13th day of the 12th month, Adar—on that very day. 12.21 Because on this day, the all-ruling The God transformed it for them from a day of destruction into [a] day of joy for the chosen race. 12.22 ‘Therefore, you yourselves are to observe this day as [a] special feast in your local celebrations, with various kinds of feasting, 12.23 so that now and in the future, it can be [a] day of salvation for us and for the Persians who support us. But for those who plot against us, it will serve as [a] memorial of their destruction. 12.24 ‘Any city or land that does not obey these decrees will be completely destroyed by spear and fire in our anger. It will become impassable for humans and utterly inhospitable to animals and birds forever.’
[Esther] [8]:[13] Copies of this were to be displayed for everyone in the kingdom to see, showing how all Judeans should prepare themselves for war against their enemies!
[Esther] [8]:[14] So, the king’s edict was carried on horseback to be quickly delivered throughout the whole realm, and it was also put on display in Susa.
[Esther] [8]:[15] Well after that, MordecAi was dressed in royal robes, and a gold crown was placed on his head over a purple turban. And when the people of Susa saw this, they all rejoiced…
[Esther] [8]:[16] And the Judeans were also very relieved and happy.
[Esther] [8]:[17] Then in every place and city where the edict had been displayed, there was rejoicing and feasting among the Judeans! And as a result (because of their fear of the Judeans), many people of the nations got circumcised and became converts to Judaism.
[Esther] [9]:[1] Well, by the 13th day of the 12th month (Adar), all the letters from the king had been distributed.
[Esther] [9]:[2] So on that day, all the enemies of the Jews were destroyed, because everyone was afraid to oppose them!
[Esther] [9]:[3] And everyone (including the heads over the governors, the vassal kings, and the royal scribes) treated the Judeans with respect, because they were afraid of MordecAi,
[Esther] [9]:[4] since the king had ordered his name
[Esther] [9]:[5] to be proclaimed throughout the kingdom.
[Esther] [9]:[6] In the city of Susa alone, the Judeans killed about 500 people,
[Esther] [9]:[7] including: PharShandatha, Daiphon, Aspatha,
[Esther] [9]:[8] Pharadatha, Barea, Sarbaka,
[Esther] [9]:[9] MarMasima, Ruphaeus, Arseus, ZabuThaeus,

[Esther] [9]:[13] And Esther said to the king: ‘Allow the Judeans to do the same thing tomorrow [here in Susa], and let them hang [up the bodies of] the 10 sons of HaMan.’
[Esther] [9]:[14] So he agreed to let it happen, and the Judeans in the city hung up the bodies of the sons of HaMan.
[Esther] [9]:[15] Then they all gathered in Susa on the 14th day of Adar and killed 300 more men… But again, they didn’t plunder them.
[Esther] [9]:[16] Meanwhile, the rest of the Judeans throughout the kingdom had also gathered to protect themselves, which finally gave them some rest from those warlike men. Altogether, they destroyed 70,000 of them on the 13th of Adar… But they didn’t do any plundering either.
[Esther] [9]:[17] Then they rested on the 14th day of the month, proclaiming it a day of rest, joy, and gladness.
[Esther] [9]:[18] The Judeans in the city of Susa also gathered for rest on the 14th day, then they celebrated on the 15th day with joy and gladness.
[Esther] [9]:[19] And because of this, all the Judeans who were scattered outside [of Judea] still celebrate the 14th day of Adar as a happy day, during which they each send food to their neighbors.
[Esther] [9]:[20] For MordecAi wrote that they should write this in a scroll that he would then send to the all Judeans throughout the kingdom of ArtaXerxes, both near and far,
[Esther] [9]:[21] establishing the 14th and 15th days of Adar as good days of celebration,
[Esther] [9]:[22] because those were the days when the Judeans were gained rest from their enemies… It was the month when their mourning was turned into joy and their grief was turned into happy days. As a result, they were to celebrate those days happily with wedding feasts and by sending food to their friends and to the poor.
[Esther] [9]:[23] The Judeans were also happy when MordecAi wrote of
[Esther] [9]:[24] how HaMan (son of HamaDathes the Macedonian) had waged war against them by authoring a referendum to wipe them out,
[Esther] [9]:[25] and of how he’d gone before the king to hang MordecAi [on a pole]. Then he told of how [HaMan’s] attempt to do bad things to the Judeans resulted in his own hanging, along with his children.
[Esther] [9]:[26] So they call those days Purim (Lots), because these were the days [that HaMan] had chosen by throwing lots (which in their dialect was called Purim). Well, because of the words in that letter, all the things that [the Jews] had suffered and that had been done to them, came to an end.
[Esther] [9]:[27] And the Judeans adopted [Purim as a holiday] for them and their offspring, and they agreed to observe it exactly as [MordecAi] suggested. It was to be a memorial from generation to generation in every city, family, and place.
[Esther] [9]:[28] These days were to be celebrated for all time, and were never to be forgotten throughout the generations!
[Esther] [9]:[29] Then Queen Esther (the daughter of AbiHail) and MordecAi (the Judean) wrote about all that they’d done, in confirmation of what was written in the letter about Purim.
[Esther] [9]:[30] MordecAi and Esther attested to all that they’d done, of how they had fasted, and to the things that they had each said.
[Esther] [9]:[31] And thereafter, Esther established the matter throughout the ages by [having it written] as a memorial.
[Esther] [10]:[1] Well after that, the king also wrote about this matter to everyone in his kingdom, both on land and at sea;
[Esther] [10]:[2] however, he also wrote about his strength, valor, riches, and the glory of his kingdom. Look! It’s all written as a memorial in the scrolls of the Persians and Medes.
[Esther] [10]:[3] [From then on,] MordecAi was second only to King ArtaXerxes and held a powerful position in the kingdom. He was highly respected by the Jews, and because he was loved, he shared his story with his entire nation. 3.1[Mordecai said:] ‘These things came from The God. 3.2‘You see, I remembered the dream I had about these events, and every single word of it came true. 3.3 The small spring that became [a] river, with light, sun, and plenty of water — well, that river is Esther, whom the king married and made queen. 3.4‘The two dragons are I and HaMan. 3.5‘The nations are those who gathered to destroy the Jewish people. 3.6‘My nation, Israel, cried out to The God and was saved. [Jehovah] saved His people and delivered us from all these evils! The God performed great signs and wonders, things no other nation had ever witnessed. 3.7‘Because of this, he cast two lots: one for [The God’s] people and one for all the nations. 3.8 These two lots occurred at the designated time, on [a] day of judgment before The God and for all the nations. 3.9‘The God remembered His people and upheld His own inheritance. 3.10 They will observe these days in the month of Adar, on the 14th and 15th of that month, with festive gatherings, joy, and gladness before The God, for all generations, into the age, among His people Israel.’ 3.11 [Note from the copyist:] In the fourth year of Ptolemy and Cleopatra’s reign, Dositheus, who claimed to be [a] priest and [a] Levite, along with his son Ptolemy, presented this letter about Purim. They said Lysimachus (Ptolemy’s son from JeruSalem) had translated it.
[Job] [1]:[1] There was a certain man named Job who lived in the land of the AuSitidi. He was true, blameless, righteous, God fearing, and he distanced himself from all that was wicked.
[Job] [1]:[2] He had seven sons, three daughters, and he also had: 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 teams of oxen, and 500 grazing female burros. In addition, he had a huge work force to serve him, and many more to care for his land...
[Job] [1]:[3] For the man had been born into a prosperous family from the sunrise in the east.
[Job] [1]:[4] [Job’s] sons prepared banquets for each other each day, and their three sisters were always invited to eat and drink with them.
[Job] [1]:[5] Then, after all the banqueting was done, Job would get up early each morning to purify them. He offered sacrifices on their behalf, which included a calf as a sin offering for their lives. As Job said: ‘[I’m doing this] just in case my children even think something bad about God.’ And that’s how Job always did things.
[Job] [1]:[6] Then one day, {Look!} the [angelic] messengers of God went to stand before [Jehovah], and the Opposer came along with them.
[Job] [1]:[7] So, [Jehovah] asked the Opposer: ‘Where have you come from?’ And the Opposer replied to [Jehovah]: ‘I’ve been on the earth, walking around everywhere under the sky.’
[Job] [1]:[8] Then [Jehovah] asked him: ‘Have you noticed and thought about My child Job? There’s no one else like him on the earth, because he’s blameless, true, God fearing, and he distances himself from anything that’s bad.’
[Job] [1]:[9] So the Opposer stood up before [Jehovah] and said: ‘Is Job really free to bow before You, [Jehovah]?
[Job] [1]:[10] ‘Haven’t You protected him and all in his household from anything that might be harmful to him? You’ve blest everything he does, and You’ve provided huge herds of cattle for him that cover the entire land!
[Job] [1]:[11] ‘However, if You were to just reach out Your hand and touch all the things that he has, then he’d surely rave against You to Your face!’
[Job] [1]:[12] Then [Jehovah] said to the Opposer: '{Look!} I’m putting everything he has into your hands… Just don’t touch him personally.’ And at that, the Opposer left the presence of [Jehovah].
[Job] [1]:[13] Well, on that day, all of Job’s sons and daughters had all been enjoying wine in the house of their older brother.
[Job] [1]:[14] But then, {Look!} a messenger came to Job and told him: ‘We were plowing with the teams of oxen, and the female burros were grazing nearby,
[Job] [1]:[15] when slavers came and took them all and killed all your servants with swords! ‘I’m the only one who escaped, so I could bring this message to you!’
[Job] [1]:[16] Then while he was still speaking, another messenger arrived and said to Job: ‘Lightning came out of the sky and burned up all the sheep! And the shepherds were destroyed the same way! ‘I’m the only one who escaped, so I came to report it to you!’
[Job] [1]:[17] And while he was still speaking, another messenger arrived and said to Job: ‘Three companies of mounted troops attacked us, then they rounded up the camels and took them, and they killed all your servants with swords! ‘I was the only one who escaped, so I’ve come to report this to you!’
[Job] [1]:[18] Well, while that one was still speaking, another messenger arrived and told Job: ‘Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking with their older brother,
[Job] [1]:[19] when a tornado came towards them from out of the desert and touched down on the four corners of his house and destroyed it, killing all your children! ‘I’m the only one who escaped, and I came to report it to you!’
[Job] [1]:[20] And with that, Job got up and started ripping his clothes, then he cut all the hair off his head, and he bowed all the way to the ground and said:
[Job] [1]:[21] ‘I came from my mother’s belly naked and I’ll return there naked… [Jehovah] gave it, and [Jehovah] took it away. ‘So, what seems good to [Jehovah] has come to pass. ‘May the Name of the Lord be praised!’
[Job] [1]:[22] Well, despite all of these terrible things that happened to him, Job didn’t sin against [Jehovah] a single time, nor did he accuse God of foolishness.
[Job] [2]:[1] Then on another day, when God’s [angelic] messengers came to stand before [Jehovah], the Opposer once more came among them to stand before the Lord.
[Job] [2]:[2] And [Jehovah] asked the Opposer: ‘So, where have you come from?’ And the Opposer again replied: ‘I’ve been on the earth, walking around everywhere under the sky.’
[Job] [2]:[3] So [Jehovah] asked him: ‘Have you been paying attention to my child Job? For there are no others like him on the earth. He’s not a wicked man… He’s true, blameless, God fearing, and he avoids anything that’s evil, so he’s still innocent. ‘However, you told me [that he wouldn’t remain faithful] if everything he had was destroyed without a reason.’
[Job] [2]:[4] Then the Opposer said to [Jehovah]: ‘Skin for skin… A man will give everything he has for his life!
[Job] [2]:[5] For a fact, if You send Your hand to touch his flesh and bones, he’ll surely rave against You to Your face!’
[Job] [2]:[6] And [Jehovah] replied to the Opposer: '{Look!} I’m giving him to you… Just don’t take his life!’
[Job] [2]:[7] So the Opposer left [Jehovah] and struck Job with terrible sores from his head to his feet.
[Job] [2]:[8] And as a result, [Job] had to carry a broken piece of pottery to scrape the pus as he sat in a pile of ashes.
[Job] [2]:[9] Then his wife asked him: ‘How much longer are you going to endure this? ‘Just speak a word to God and end it!’
[Job] [2]:[10] But he looked at her and said: ‘Why are you acting like such a foolish woman? If we’ve looked for good things from the hand of [Jehovah], shouldn’t we also endure the bad?’
[Job] [2]:[11] Then, when three of his friends heard of all the bad things that had happened to him, they each came from their lands to see him. There was: EliPhaz the Temanite (a king), Baldad the Shuhite (a sovereign ruler), and Zophar the Minaean (a king). They had all come to visit him for the purpose of comforting him.
[Job] [2]:[12] However, as they approached, they didn’t even recognize him! So they each started shouting, crying, ripping their clothes, and throwing dust in the air.
[Job] [2]:[13] Then they all sat down beside him for seven days and seven nights without speaking a word... For they recognized that this was a terrible calamity, which was much worse than anything they’d anticipated.
[Job] [3]:[1] Well, after this, Job opened his mouth and cursed his day,
[Job] [3]:[2] saying:
[Job] [3]:[3] ‘May the day I was born be destroyed, Along with the night when they said, It’s a boy!
[Job] [3]:[4] ‘May that night become very dark... May the Lord up above never seek it, And may it not see the coming of dawn.
[Job] [3]:[5] May it be taken by darkness And by the shadow of death. ‘May that day forever be dimmed… May that day forever be cursed,
[Job] [3]:[6] And its night carried into the darkness. ‘No more, may it be a day of the year, Nor may it be counted in one of the months.
[Job] [3]:[7] May that night become one of grieving, Not one who is happy and joyful.
[Job] [3]:[8] ‘May the One who brought a curse to that day Also heap curses upon it. May it be [swallowed by] beasts of the sea
[Job] [3]:[9] And may darkness cover the stars of that night, So they’ll no longer be seen… And may they not shine ever after. ‘May the morning star not arise,
[Job] [3]:[10] For it failed to close the womb of my mother, So my eyes wouldn’t see all of this misery.
[Job] [3]:[11] ‘Why didn’t I die in her belly Instead of having to ever be born? Why wasn’t I killed there and then?
[Job] [3]:[12] Why did her knees come to meet me, And why did her breasts come to nurse me?
[Job] [3]:[13] ‘May I go to my bed and lie still…
[Job] [3]:[14] May I sleep and find rest among kings… The councilors of the lands where they once pranced with swords…
[Job] [3]:[15] With the rulers that once had so much gold And that once filled their houses with silver.
[Job] [3]:[16] ‘O if I’d just been miscarried Within the womb of my mother, Like babies that don’t see light of day,
[Job] [3]:[17] And go where the anger and rage of the Godless Has all been burned up in fire. ‘It’s that place where the tired find rest for their bones,
[Job] [3]:[18] And where none that have lived throughout the ages Hear tax collector’s voices again.
[Job] [3]:[19] It’s where the small and the great must all go… The servants [along with] their masters.
[Job] [3]:[20] ‘Why must those who are bitter see light, And why is life given to those who are grieved,
[Job] [3]:[21] Then long for death that won’t come… Those rooting for death as though it were treasure,
[Job] [3]:[22] And who’d be overjoyed to attain it?
[Job] [3]:[23] ‘For to such a man, death becomes rest, When there’s nowhere else he can go… Yes, when [our] God has opposed him.
[Job] [3]:[24] ‘My grain has now become groaning, And I’m crying and shaking in fear;
[Job] [3]:[25] For the things I once feared in my dreams have come true, And what I held in awe has now met me.
[Job] [3]:[26] I’m not at peace, or still, or at rest, For [His] rage has now come upon me.’
[Job] [4]:[1] Then EliPhaz the Temanite decided to speak. He said:
[Job] [4]:[2] ‘Do you often complain of your problems? Who can stand such strong talk?
[Job] [4]:[3] ‘To many people, you’ve given advice, And to the hands of the weak, you’ve brought comfort;
[Job] [4]:[4] You’ve lifted the timid with words, And encouraged the ones who had feeble knees.
[Job] [4]:[5] But now that this misery has arrived to touch you, You tend to be in a hurry!
[Job] [4]:[6] ‘Aren’t you rather in fear of your own foolish ways… Your own wrong hopes and bad paths?
[Job] [4]:[7] Can you think of any who are truly pure That [God has] ever destroyed, Or any of the true who have been wiped away?
[Job] [4]:[8] ‘I’ve seen people who plow in strange places, And those who plant there, reap grief for themselves.
[Job] [4]:[9] Then, by [God’s] order, they perish… With the spirit of His wrath, they’re then wiped away.
[Job] [4]:[10] ‘So the strength of the lion and the lioness’ roar, And the prancing of beasts is no more.
[Job] [4]:[11] Like the lion’s cubs that die without prey, The young won’t come to each other’s aid.
[Job] [4]:[12] ‘So, if the things that you said are all true, And if they’ve all really happened; Then, none of these things would’ve happened to you. ‘Should my ears now start to believe That He’s done something so strange?
[Job] [4]:[13] ‘An echo in the night brings fear to all men…
[Job] [4]:[14] It stuns them, makes them tremble, and rattles their bones.
[Job] [4]:[15] But a spirit once came and looked in my face, Which made my flesh shudder and my hair stand erect.
[Job] [4]:[16] I jumped, for I didn’t understand what I saw; But, there it was in front of my eyes. ‘Then I felt a breeze and I heard a voice say:
[Job] [4]:[17] Why should a man be pure before God? For He doesn’t even trust His own servants, And He thinks of His angels as crooked.
[Job] [4]:[19] ‘Those who live in houses of clay Are made from its very same mortar; So, both are destroyed in the very same way.
[Job] [4]:[20] [They come] in the morning, then by evening, are gone… And they die, if they can’t help themselves. ‘He just breathes upon them and they wither… They perish in their own foolish ways.’
[Job] [5]:[1] ‘So, shout and see who’ll listen; Will holy angels appear?
[Job] [5]:[2] Even a fool will end all his madness, And a man who wanders will soon end his search.
[Job] [5]:[3] ‘I’ve seen fools making plans… And then, their homes were destroyed.
[Job] [5]:[4] And although their sons were in a safe place, At the doors of lesser men, they were crushed; For, no one would come to their aid.
[Job] [5]:[5] ‘Even though the hungry can eat what they harvest; Those who bear arms can siphon their strength.
[Job] [5]:[6] So the ground will only bring work, As misery sprouts in the hills.
[Job] [5]:[7] ‘Even though a man is just born to do work, And young vultures are made to fly in the skies;
[Job] [5]:[8] I’ll still beg to [Jehovah]… Yes, I’ll still call to the Almighty God
[Job] [5]:[9] Who does great things that can’t be explained… Things of honor, unnumbered, and odd.
[Job] [5]:[10] ‘He’s the One who sends water down to the ground And rain to all places under the skies.
[Job] [5]:[11] He’s the One who raises the humble And returns life to those who are dying.
[Job] [5]:[12] ‘He alters the plans of the clever, So that they’re unable to do what’s true.
[Job] [5]:[13] He conquers the wisdom of the wise, And surprises the plans of the crafty.
[Job] [5]:[14] ‘For, in daylight, darkness can still come to meet them, And at noon, they may grope as though it were night.
[Job] [5]:[15] They may also be killed in a war, While the weak may escape from the mighty.
[Job] [5]:[16] ‘So, there’s still hope for those without strength, And unrighteous mouths may also be closed.
[Job] [5]:[17] ‘Blest is the man who has been whipped by the Lord, And those who don’t ignore the Almighty!
[Job] [5]:[18] For, although He brings pain, He also restores… He strikes, and then He heals with His hands.
[Job] [5]:[19] ‘Six times, He will save you from problems, But in the seventh, He will give you what’s bad.
[Job] [5]:[20] In times of famine, He will save you from death; And in war, He will free you from shackles of iron.
[Job] [5]:[21] From the whip of the tongue, He will hide you, And you won’t have to fear the evils that come.
[Job] [5]:[22] ‘Then you’ll laugh at the unrighteous and lawless, And not have fear of any wild beasts.
[Job] [5]:[23] For with you, the wild will be peaceful,
[Job] [5]:[24] And you’ll know there’s peace in your house When you tent in your home without sin.
[Job] [5]:[25] ‘You’ll know that your offspring will be many, And your children will sprout like weeds in the fields.
[Job] [5]:[26] Then you’ll go to your grave like grain in the harvest… Like heaps on the floor at the time it’s reaped.
[Job] [5]:[27] '{Look!} These are the things that we’ve concluded, And these are the things that we’ve heard. But, within yourself, only you know Whether you’ve done something evil.’
[Job] [6]:[1] Then Job spoke. He said:
[Job] [6]:[2] ‘If you’d use a balancing scale To measure my anger against all my grief, You’d find that they both balance out…
[Job] [6]:[3] But they’re still as heavy as the sands of the seas. ‘For it seems as though you’ve not heard what I’ve said…
[Job] [6]:[4] That my body has been pierced by God’s arrows… That His rage has been drinking my blood, And this stings me whenever I’m starting to speak.
[Job] [6]:[5] ‘Why do wild burros cry out When they aren’t looking for grain? And why do cattle bawl from their stables When there’s plenty of grain?
[Job] [6]:[6] ‘As bread should be eaten with salt; What taste can be found in your empty words?
[Job] [6]:[7] Yet, I still can’t drive them out of my life. ‘Now I groan when I see my cereal grains; For [to me], they have the odor of lions.
[Job] [6]:[8] ‘If He would just give me the things that I ask… If the Lord would just give me the things that I’ve hoped…
[Job] [6]:[9] But, [Jehovah] has started to pierce me, And it’s not been withdrawn or come to its end!
[Job] [6]:[10] ‘So if the place of the dead could now be my city, Upon its walls I’d jump… Yes, I’d gladly accept it.
[Job] [6]:[11] ‘Since I haven’t lied about God’s holy words, Why have I still got the strength to remain… Why do I have the strength to live on?
[Job] [6]:[12] Am I as mighty as the rocks… Are my body parts made of bronze?
[Job] [6]:[13] ‘In Him, have I not put my trust? Yet His help has been taken away!
[Job] [6]:[14] Has His mercy to me been forbidden, And have the visits of the Lord overlooked me?
[Job] [6]:[15] ‘Those closest to me, now see me no more, For I’m like a stream that’s gone dry, Or a wave that’s already passed by; For now, everyone just walks past me.
[Job] [6]:[16] ‘Those who once showed deep respect Now view me like banks of ice or of snow
[Job] [6]:[17] That has melted away in the heat [of the day], And no longer is seen as what it once was.
[Job] [6]:[18] That’s how I’ve been abandoned by all… I’m destroyed and I’ve become homeless.
[Job] [6]:[19] ‘Behold the Temanite trails And all the passes of the Sabaeans, O you, who now think that you’re seeing things clearly.
[Job] [6]:[20] They [exist because of] those living in towns, And they’re the things that they rely upon there.
[Job] [6]:[21] ‘Now, with no mercy, you all stand [away], As if you’re afraid of my sores.
[Job] [6]:[22] Yet, what have I asked you to give me? And how much of your strength have I asked for?
[Job] [6]:[23] Just save me from my enemy’s hands, And snatch me away from the mighty!
[Job] [6]:[24] ‘Teach me, and I’ll then remain silent… If I’ve strayed, then prove it!
[Job] [6]:[25] For, you view the words of someone who is true As though they’ve become very foul. ‘I haven’t asked for your strength,
[Job] [6]:[26] And your scolding won’t stop me from speaking. I won’t put up with the things that you say;
[Job] [6]:[27] For you’re coming down on an orphan, And you’re attacking a friend!
[Job] [6]:[28] ‘Now, as I gaze at your faces, I’ll tell you no lies.
[Job] [6]:[29] So, just sit here and don’t be unrighteous… Just sit here together with one who is just;
[Job] [6]:[30] For, nothing wrong has come from my tongue, And from my throat will come things to consider.’
[Job] [7]:[1] ‘The purpose of man on the earth Is surely not just to be tried. For he lives his life as a hired day worker,
[Job] [7]:[2] And as a servant in awe of his master… One who stands in the shade of his shadow As he’s awaiting his wages.
[Job] [7]:[3] ‘Thus, for months, I’ve waited in vain, To only receive nights of grief.
[Job] [7]:[4] For, when I go to bed, I now say: How long will it be ‘til day comes again? And thereafter, I must ask when I rise, How soon will it become night? ‘I’m filled with grief from morning ‘til night;
[Job] [7]:[5] For my body is rotting and covered with worms. Like clods of dirt, I’m melting away, As I’m scraping away all the pus.
[Job] [7]:[6] My life now weighs less than my words … It has perished in hopes unattained.
[Job] [7]:[7] ‘My soul has become like a breeze, And my eyes no longer see good.
[Job] [7]:[8] The eyes of those searching, don’t see me… Even though their eyes are upon me, I’m gone
[Job] [7]:[9] Like a cloud that drifts away in the sky.
[Job] [7]:[10] ‘When a man goes down to his grave, He doesn’t come back again. There’s no way he will return to his house… For, even his home doesn’t know him.
[Job] [7]:[11] But, I’ll not close my mouth… Yes, I’ll still speak of my plight. I’ll bear open my soul To show you the bitterness it holds…
[Job] [7]:[12] I won’t be like the sea’s dragons.
[Job] [7]:[13] ‘I once said that my bed brings me comfort. But now, all I have to offer myself Are my own words, as I lie on my cot,
[Job] [7]:[14] Where I’m frightened by dreams And by visions that strike me with terror.
[Job] [7]:[15] ‘[Please] let my breath leave my soul, And may my bones be handed to death!
[Job] [7]:[16] May I no longer live in [this] age… For, why must I just keep on waiting, When all in my life is so empty?
[Job] [7]:[17] ‘O what’s a man that You’d make him so great, Or notice the things that he thinks?
[Job] [7]:[18] Why visit him until morning arrives And judge him as he lies there asleep?
[Job] [7]:[19] ‘How long will [You] keep me alive And refuse to provide my release, As I swallow my spit in my grief?
[Job] [7]:[20] ‘If I’ve sinned, then what can I do, O You who knows the minds of all men? Why have You made me [a person] who blames You, And why have You made me Your burden?
[Job] [7]:[21] ‘Why not rather forget the laws that I broke, And then cleanse me from all of my sins? Please let me go into the ground, And no longer rise early again.’
[Job] [8]:[1] Then Baldad the Shuhite spoke. He said:
[Job] [8]:[2] ‘How long will you use the breath from your mouth To speak in such a talkative way?
[Job] [8]:[3] ‘Does [Jehovah] sin when He judges, And does the Maker of all harm the righteous?
[Job] [8]:[4] Surely your sons had sinned before Him… Because they were lawless, He took them away!
[Job] [8]:[5] ‘To seek [Jehovah], you always rose early, And before the Almighty, you’ve begged.
[Job] [8]:[6] But, if you were truly pure, He’d have listened to all your requests And restored your position in justice.
[Job] [8]:[7] Then, if at first, your men had been few; In the end, they’d be beyond number.

[Job] [8]:[9] For, while they were here, they were not aware That shadows would cover their lives in the ground.

[Job] [8]:[14] His home won’t be lived in again, And spiders will spread out their tents there.
